title: Omuramba
author: Kaaka Kyomuhendo
desc: Brown omugusha sorghum mixed with wood ash and soaked twenty-four hours in the dark until it blackens and sprouts, sun-dried, ground on a rubengo stone, then mixed with warm water and kept seven days in a cool room.
longDesc: Omuramba is the sorghum drink the Bakiga make in preparation for the cold months of June and July, and it is what enturire is built on. The ash is believed to control the final taste — a different claim from enturire's tannin argument, and both are documented. The sprouted grain is called amamera, and the grinding stone a rubengo. Seven days in a cool room is the whole fermentation, and it is served at every community event, mostly to older men, in wooden cups.
ingredients: Brown sorghum, the omugusha variety, harvested and dried
steps: Harvest and dry the brown omugusha sorghum.
Mix it with wood ashes, which is believed to control the final taste.
Soak it in clean water for 24 hours, in darkness, so it blackens and sprouts into amamera.
Sun-dry the sprouted grain, then winnow it.
Grind it to powder on a grinding stone, the rubengo.
Mix the powder with warm water.
Keep it seven days in a cool room before drinking.
chefTips: Twenty-four hours in the dark, and the grain blackens and sprouts. Both changes together tell you the soak is done — the sprouted grain has its own name, amamera.
Warm water for the fermentation, not hot and not cold. That is what the source specifies.
Seven days in a cool room. Only moderately low temperatures are documented, so a cool larder rather than a refrigerator.

The ash here is said to control the final taste. In enturire, the same ash is credited with removing tannins and improving flavour, aroma and colour. Both claims are documented and they are not incompatible.
Grind it properly to powder. The rubengo stone gives a finer result than a hand mill and the texture of the drink depends on it.
The Bakiga prepare it for the cold months of June and July and regard it as an energy drink and an immunity booster. That is their framing and it is worth passing on as theirs.
It is omuramba that enturire is built on, so making this first is the best way to understand UGA089.
No flour-to-water ratio is documented, and no temperature beyond moderately low.
commonMistakes: Using hot water for the fermentation.
sources: Adapted from the omuramba Ark of Taste entry of the Slow Food Foundation — the brown omugusha sorghum, the mixing with wood ashes believed to control the final taste, the 24-hour soak in clean water in darkness producing the blackened sprouted amamera, the sun-drying and winnowing, the grinding to powder on the rubengo stone, the mixing with warm water and the seven days in a cool room are all from that entry, along with the moderately low temperature, the Kigezi and Kabale District attribution, the Bakiga preparing it for the cold months of June and July, their framing of it as an energy drink and immunity booster, and its service at every community event and gathering to old people mostly men.

The WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004 records omuramba as sorghum-based, mostly consumed by people from Kigezi in south-western Uganda, and normally taken in wooden cups at marriage ceremonies, parties and other social gatherings.
No flour-to-water ratio and no fermentation temperature beyond 'moderately low' are documented.
storage: Drunk after its seven days. It keeps some days beyond that.
healthBenefits: Sorghum is high in fibre, iron, magnesium and B vitamins.
Sprouting raises the available sugars and lowers the tannins.
Fermentation adds lactic acid bacteria and improves mineral absorption.
Regarded locally as an energy drink and an immunity booster, which is a community claim rather than a measured one.
culturalNote: Brewing something specifically in preparation for June and July — Kigezi's cold months, high in the south-western hills — is the kind of seasonal logic that gets lost when a cuisine is written up as a list of dishes. That it is served mostly to older men is also worth recording plainly rather than smoothing over.
